content: There are two types of nucleic acid testing (NAT) for hepatitis B virus (HBV): qualitative and quantitative. Qualitative NAT provides binary results, indicating whether HBV DNA is detectable or undetectable. Quantitative NAT, on the other hand, measures the HBV DNA levels and provides a continuous value. In studies where quantitative NAT results were used, the HBV DNA levels were dichotomized into high and low categories based on a specific threshold defined by each study. To ensure consistency, the threshold for defining high HBV DNA levels was required to be at least 20,000 IU/mL or higher. For studies using qualitative NAT, the limit of detection for the test was also required to be at least 20,000 IU/mL. For example, in cases where HBV DNA levels were ≥200,000 IU/mL, sensitivity and specificity were calculated as follows: sensitivity was defined as the proportion of women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL who tested positive for HBeAg, divided by the total number of women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL. Specificity was defined as the proportion of women with HBV DNA <200,000 IU/mL who tested negative for HBeAg, divided by the total number of women with HBV DNA <200,000 IU/mL. To calculate these estimates, studies needed to provide sufficient data to construct 2x2 or 2x1 tables, cross-classifying reference test results (high vs. low HBV DNA levels) with index test results (positive vs. negative HBeAg serostatus). The outcomes of the studies were stratified based on the type of preventive measures provided, such as timely administration of a birth dose vaccine and hepatitis B immunoglobulin (HBIG) at birth. Only studies that allowed sensitivity and specificity estimates to be stratified by these preventive measures were included. Studies involving antiviral therapy for mothers during pregnancy were excluded, as the objective was to evaluate HBV markers as tools to identify pregnant women who might benefit from antiviral therapy during pregnancy. Studies were included regardless of design, language, or publication date, provided they used an HBV DNA threshold of at least 20,000 IU/mL to dichotomize HBV DNA levels. Additionally, studies needed to provide sufficient data to construct cross-classifications of reference and index test results in pregnant women with chronic hepatitis B (CHB) who were not receiving concurrent anti-HBV therapy. Studies published between January 1, 2000, and April 3, 2019, were considered. To avoid verification bias, studies that selected participants based on maternal HBeAg status or viral load were excluded. The search strategy included terms such as hepatitis B infection, viral load, and pregnancy, and was applied to multiple databases, including PubMed, EMBASE, Scopus, CENTRAL, CNKI, and Wanfang. Manual searches of references from included studies and relevant systematic reviews were also conducted. Expert opinions were sought to identify additional eligible studies. Titles and abstracts of identified publications were independently screened by two reviewers for relevance. Full-text articles of potentially eligible studies were then reviewed. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. For Chinese databases, the same procedure was followed by two independent Chinese reviewers. If information was missing from the full-text articles, corresponding authors were contacted for clarification. The quality of included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers using the QUADAS-2 tool, which evaluates the risk of bias and applicability of the population, index test, and reference test to the main review questions. Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a pre-piloted data extraction form. In cases of disagreement, a third reviewer was consulted. Articles from the same study site with overlapping recruitment periods, enrollment criteria, and treatment types were considered part of a single study. If overlap was confirmed, only the most recent publication was used for data analysis. Sensitivity and specificity were estimated at various HBV DNA thresholds (e.g., ≥20,000 IU/mL, ≥5 log10 IU/mL, ≥6 log10 IU/mL, etc.). If a single study reported results at multiple thresholds, all thresholds were included. For studies allowing estimation of both sensitivity and specificity, bivariate analysis was performed. Summary statistics were pooled when at least three studies were available. Positive and negative likelihood ratios (PLR and NLR) were calculated from pooled sensitivity and specificity. Heterogeneity across studies was assessed visually using forest plots and summary scatter plots, and statistically using variables such as assay type, reference standard, maternal age, virological characteristics, and WHO region. The quality of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE methodology, which considers factors such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Evidence was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low quality. Decisions were made through consensus among study group reviewers, with support from a WHO-designated methodological expert. The search strategy identified 9,001 papers, of which 82 were included in the final review. Reasons for exclusion are detailed in the study flowchart. Sensitivity and specificity of HBeAg testing to identify women with high HBV DNA viral loads were analyzed, and detailed characteristics of included studies are presented in the supplementary materials.
